comment: I get what you’re saying. If it’s specific it may make everything a little easier, thus, people won’t turn off their alerts. But kidnappers don’t really leave a lot of clues you know. Sometimes it is difficult to pin point where the kid could have been picked up. Or where the kidnapper (be it a parent or someone random) could be heading towards. Honestly, I wouldn’t be surprised if a kid is picked up at location A and been taken to location B which could be an hour or 2 or even 3 hours away( no one’s going to stay in one location if they plan on taking away a child). Wouldn’t then it be obvious for people surrounding a town that maybe be even 300 miles away receive an amber alert. Definitely, no one likes getting 5 to 10 alerts per day. But if it were like this - either you get an alert or not. I would choose to get one, because you never really know if you could end up helping someone. Again, I don’t think people who are complaining about amber alerts don’t want to help kids, I don’t think that at all. No one is that selfish, I get it. But to turn off your alerts, or have such a huge issue with it. It’s a little too much. I see comments where people say it’s just another parent who took away the kid. Family dispute only and blah blah blah. But that still could be very dangerous, you never know if the kid is actually safe. A lot of these kids that are picked up by another parent are never found. Many of them even murdered or taken away by abusive individuals. Just the thought of that is scary. So yeah, I may be a little naive and very optimistic about these annoying alerts.. but out of 10 not very specific alerts, if even one or two could actually help out a kid in need, I’d be cool with it. Without a thought or doubt, I’d be cool with it. 😅

comment:
The reason I turned off amber alerts is probably the same reason most people do— we live in a state larger than a significant number of countries.  Amber alerts should be more targeted.  I don’t need to know 10 minutes after a child goes missing in El Paso.  

In healthcare, there’s something called “alarm fatigue.”  The premise is that when call bells in the hospital go off very frequently, response times increase less because of the time to actually respond to a call than because you become desensitized.

I’m not saying that there isn’t a child missing and that we shouldn’t alert people, but we should be selective as to not inundate people. comment:
If we got alerts every time someone’s child went missing, you wouldn’t even be able to use your phone.

There’s billboards, highway signs, news stations, news apps, social media, and many more ways to better communicate a missing child and the danger they are in. The reason people are upset is because many people have turned off amber alerts due to the frequency and unnecessary emergency alert noise especially when many of them stem from custody battles where the child is likely in no real danger.

A public safety alert is meant to convey a danger to public safety like a chemical spill, downed power lines, 911 outage, active shooter, or major accident. Sending an amber alert through the public safety alert category makes people turn those off now too and inhibits them from receiving potentially life saving information in a matter of seconds when seconds matter as opposed to wait 15-20 or more minutes for the news media to pick it up and relay the info.

The blue alert that went out last month went out as an emergency alert which is to alert people to imminent danger such as tornadoes, flash flooding, or widespread power outages. That should’ve gone out as a public safety alert within a 10-25 mile radius instead of to the whole state where people can actually keep their eye out.
